title: leaving Vrindavan

segments.voice: Yesterday: rasa lila ended. The search, the song by the river, and the circle, with Krishna between every two gopis.

A chariot is on the road to Vraja, and its driver is carrying a trap. King Kamsa of Mathura has learned that the cowherd boy everyone talks about is the son he was warned of, the one born to kill him. So Kamsa plans a festival: a contest of wrestlers, and an elephant at the gate. All he needs is someone the boys will trust to bring them. He chooses Akrura, a respected elder of their own clan. Akrura agrees to go.
screen: `A CHARIOT CARRYING A TRAP.` → `KAMSA NEEDS A MESSENGER.` → `AKRURA AGREES TO GO.`

segments.voice: Here's the surprise. Akrura is Kamsa's messenger, and Krishna's devotee. The Bhagavata spends the whole ride inside his head, and what's there isn't dread. It's longing. All the way he turns one thought over: I'm going to see him. Will Krishna look at him kindly, or hold him at arm's length as the king's man? He counts the long errand as good fortune, because of where it ends. He reaches Vraja at sunset, as the cows come home. In the dust of the cow pen he sees footprints, and knows whose they are; the text says they carry the marks devotees look for on the soles of Krishna's feet. Akrura jumps down from his chariot and rolls in that dust, overcome. Then Krishna and Balarama come out to meet him. No arm's length. The brothers embrace him, take his hand, lead him in, wash his feet and feed him. Krishna asks after his family, and only then asks what brought him. And Akrura, the king's messenger, tells them everything: Kamsa's hatred, the festival, the plan. Krishna and Balarama laugh, and agree to go. Two loyalties ride in that chariot, and the story doesn't scold him for either. It lets us watch a man doing a hard errand with his heart pointed somewhere else.
screen: `THE KING'S MAN, AND KRISHNA'S DEVOTEE.` · `FOOTPRINTS IN THE DUST.` · `WASHED, FED, ASKED AFTER.` · then, large: `HE TELLS THEM EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one errand ahead that you'd rather not do, and hold it lightly. Then look past it, the way Akrura looked down the road, to who or what waits at the end, and breathe with that; you don't have to love the errand. If you pray, you can offer it to God, or to Krishna, before you begin.
Leaving Vrindavan. The turn in the Bhagavata when Akrura comes from Mathura with Kamsa's summons, and Krishna agrees to go.
Your line: Akrura in the dust. He carried the king's summons and spent the road hoping. Day nine hundred two.

howItsDone: Akrura is remembered by devotees as a model of longing to see God; the chapters of his journey to Vraja are recited from the Bhagavata, and pilgrims to the Vrindavan area visit places linked with the story.

chat.meaning: Akrura was Kamsa's messenger and Krishna's devotee. He rode with longing, rolled in Krishna's footprints, and told the brothers Kamsa's plan.
